study.title: Acupuncture Enhances Effective Connectivity between Cerebellum and Primary Sensorimotor Cortex in Patients with Stable Recovery Stroke
study.study_design: Observational fMRI study with within-subject repeated measures; stroke patients and healthy controls underwent three runs of fMRI scan (resting state before acupuncture, acupuncture run, passive finger movement); 8 patients underwent the experiment twice at an interval of two weeks
study.blinding: Subjects were not informed of the presumed acupuncture effects; no formal blinding procedure described
study.population: Stroke patients with hemiparetic upper extremity deficits and age-matched healthy controls
study.disease_condition: Ischemic stroke (stable recovery/subacute phase) with unilateral right-sided striatocapsular lesions and moderate to severe motor deficits of the contralesional upper extremity
study.inclusion_criteria: (1) >2 and <12 weeks from the onset of ischemic stroke; (2) unilateral right-sided striatocapsular lesions; (3) Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) score >= 21; (4) moderate to severe motor deficits of the contralesional upper extremity, Motricity Index (MI) < 80; (5) right-handed individuals according to the Edinburgh Handedness; (6) age range of 35–75 y. [For healthy controls:] age-matched and sexually matched, right-handed individuals, no history of drug abuse, alcohol abuse, stroke, or other neurological or psychiatric diseases.
study.exclusion_criteria: (1) any clinically significant or unstable medical disorder, (2) bihemispheric or brain stem infarcts; (3) severe aphasia precluding communication, (4) any neuropsychiatric comorbidity other than stroke, and (5) standard contraindications for MRI such as non-MRI compatible implanted metallic devices

extraction_notes.note: The paper reports that 8 patients underwent the experiment twice (two weeks apart) and 1 patient only once, but the imaging analyses appear to treat each session or average across sessions without explicitly stating how repeated measurements from the same subject were handled in the mGCA. The exact number of data points entering each analysis is unclear.
No sham or placebo acupuncture condition was included. The study compares stroke patients to healthy controls receiving the same real acupuncture. There is no sham arm.

Coordinates (MNI or Talairach) are not provided for any brain regions. ROIs are defined using the Talairach-Daemon-based atlas and referred to by anatomical label only. No peak or cluster coordinate tables are presented.

The paper states ROIs were defined from healthy group motor task activation (P < 0.05, FDR corrected), but no specific activation coordinate table is presented. The list of ROIs is provided in narrative/text form only.

In Table 1, two rows of values are shown for each clinical measure per patient. The paper states 8 patients underwent the experiment twice and 1 patient once, but it is unclear whether the rows represent two MRI sessions or two clinical assessment timepoints, or whether these are identical. The paper says 'All patients recruited were scored on the following function measures on the same day as MRI.'

The exact correction method for the path weight comparisons in Tables 2 and 3 is not fully described beyond 'P < 0.05' and 'P < 0.01'. It is unclear whether these are corrected for multiple comparisons across all ROI pairs.

Region abbreviations used in Tables 2 and 3 (e.g., 'Postcentral GR', 'Postcentral GL', 'Precentral GL', 'Precentral GR', 'P Thalamus', 'MCC', 'IPL', 'SubN', 'STG', 'MTG', 'ACC') are not fully defined in a legend within the tables. Definitions were inferred from the main text and figure labels. 'GR' likely means right, 'GL' likely means left; 'MCC' = middle cingulate cortex; 'P Thalamus' = posterior thalamus; 'IPL' = inferior parietal lobule; 'SubN' = substantia nigra; 'STG' = superior temporal gyrus; 'MTG' = middle temporal gyrus; 'ACC' = anterior cingulate cortex.
Expectancy, credibility, and allocation guessing were not formally assessed or reported.
The duration of de qi sensation after needle removal is explicitly acknowledged as a limitation: 'it is hard to record for how long de qi sensation lasted after acupuncture stimulation.'

The coordinate space is stated as MNI (normalization to MNI template), but the ROI atlas used is described as 'standard Talairach-Daemon-based atlas.' This creates ambiguity about whether the final ROI coordinates would be in MNI or Talairach space. No explicit coordinate values are provided anywhere in the paper, so this does not affect coordinate extraction but is noted for context.

The paper refers to 'culmen' as a cerebellar region (anterior vermis, part of spinocerebellum). In Figure 2, both 'Declive' and 'Culmen' appear as nodes. 'Culmen' corresponds to culmen (anterior lobe of cerebellum) and 'Declive' to declive (posterior lobe). These are both cerebellar structures distinct from each other.

Figure 2 provides visual representations of causal connectivity networks for all conditions and groups, but no numerical values (path weights, DTF values) are readable from the figure. Edge thicknesses indicate strength qualitatively only.

The paper states 'For bilaterally activated areas, time series were averaged' during ROI definition. This means some ROI entries in Tables 2 and 3 (e.g., 'Culmen', 'Declive', 'Insula', 'MTG', 'IPL', etc.) may represent averaged bilateral signals, while others (Postcentral GL, Postcentral GR, Precentral GL, Precentral GR) represent hemisphere-specific regions. The exact list of which were averaged bilaterally is not provided.
